passage: It's been a month since Salma and I sat down with our manager and wrote out the agreement, and I, Kiran, didn't expect it to hold. Three lines on one page: Salma owns client calls, I own the analysis; both names go on every deck, in alphabetical order; if something bothers either of us, we say it within two days, privately. Honestly, the third line was the hardest. Two weeks in, Salma moved a deadline without telling me, and the old me would have stewed for a month. Instead I messaged: 'Can we talk about Thursday?' It took ten minutes. Yesterday we had our one-month check-in over chai. We both laughed at how much energy we'd wasted being silently angry. Next time I'll speak up in week one, not month three.

qa.q: Whose names go on every deck, and in what order?
qa.a: Both names go on every deck, in alphabetical order.

qa.q: Why was the third line of the agreement the hardest for Kiran?
qa.a: Speaking up within two days went against Kiran's old habit of stewing silently, so it felt uncomfortable and risky.

qa.q: What made this agreement actually work?
qa.a: It was short and specific about ownership, credit and raising concerns, and it was tested early with a ten-minute talk and a one-month check-in.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt receiving 'Can we talk about Thursday?'
qa.a: Salma may have felt a moment of worry but also relief that the issue came directly and quickly, rather than turning into weeks of coldness.

grounding: Two colleagues agree on ownership, shared credit and raising concerns early, check in after a month, and see the conflict as a lesson in speaking sooner.

Supervisor's note, Raghav, one month after the Hemant and Nisha agreement.
What they agreed in March: Hemant owns vendor contracts, Nisha owns the budget sheet; credit on reports names both, with each person's part listed; any concern gets raised within the week, first with each other, then with me if needed.
What I saw: two emails this month opened with 'Flagging early...' One from Nisha about a late invoice, one from Hemant about a formula. Both were sorted the same day. The team report went out with a short line under each section: who did what.
At today's check-in, Hemant said, 'If we'd done this in January, we'd have saved ourselves the shouting.' Nisha nodded.
Next: suggest the whole team uses the same ownership sheet.

qa.q: What did Nisha's early email flag?
qa.a: A late invoice.

qa.q: What does Hemant's comment about January suggest about Hemant's thinking now?
qa.a: Hemant seems to regret not speaking up sooner and sees the conflict as a lesson in raising concerns early.

qa.q: Why is Raghav's next step, sharing the ownership sheet, a good idea?
qa.a: It spreads what worked, clear ownership and early flagging, so the rest of the team can prevent similar conflicts.

qa.q: How might Nisha experience a report that lists who did what?
qa.a: Nisha likely feels the work is visible and fairly credited, which builds trust instead of resentment.

grounding: A supervisor records how clear ownership, shared credit and early flagging held up at a one-month check-in, turning a past clash into a lesson.

passage:
Diary, 2 December
One month since Zainab and I sat with our manager and wrote everything down. Today we did our check-in, in the small meeting room, twenty minutes.
What we agreed then: I own client research, she owns the proposals, both names go on every deck, and if something bugs either of us, we say it within a day, privately.
What actually happened: mostly good! Both names were on the last two decks. Once I forgot to update the tracker and Zainab told me the same afternoon, calmly, instead of fuming for a week. Once I told her she'd changed my numbers without asking. She said sorry.
Looking back, the whole fight could have been a two-minute conversation in March.
Mahima

qa.q: How long was Mahima and Zainab's check-in?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel about the month, judging by the diary?
qa.a: Mahima feels relieved and a little rueful, pleased the agreements work while regretting the fight wasn't raised sooner.

qa.q: What makes the agreements work in practice?
qa.a: Clear ownership, both names on every deck, and raising concerns within a day, privately.

qa.q: How might Zainab see the month since the agreement?
qa.a: Zainab likely feels more respected, since the numbers issue and the tracker were both handled quickly and calmly.

grounding: Shows two colleagues checking in a month after agreeing ownership, shared credit and early concerns, and seeing the value of speaking up sooner.

passage:
At the sugar cooperative office in Kolhapur, the whiteboard by the door now had two columns: PARVEEN, farmer payments. RAFIQ, mill schedule. Underneath, in Rafiq's handwriting: Both names on every report. Problems: tell each other same day.
It had been a month since the manager helped them write it. On Friday afternoon, Parveen pulled up a chair next to Rafiq's desk.
"Check-in time."
They went down the list. Both names had gone on three reports. Rafiq admitted he'd once changed her payment dates without asking; she'd told him within the hour. "That would have been a war, before," he said.
Parveen laughed. "We should have spoken up in the first week."

qa.q: What was written under the two columns on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Both names on every report. Problems: tell each other same day.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he said it would have been a war before?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and a bit amused, glad the agreement stopped a small problem from turning into a fight.

qa.q: Why does writing the agreement on the whiteboard help the follow-through?
qa.a: It keeps ownership, shared credit and same-day concerns visible every day, so both can check themselves.

qa.q: How does Parveen see the conflict now?
qa.a: Parveen sees it as a lesson, laughing that they should have spoken up in the first week.

grounding: Shows colleagues following up a month after agreeing ownership, credit and early concerns, learning to speak up sooner.

passage: The sheet Omar and Anders had written together was still pinned above the coffee machine in the museum workshop in Gothenburg: "Omar owns lighting and labels. Anders owns layout and the loan paperwork. Both names on every exhibit plan. If something bugs you, say it within two days, not two months." A month later, on a grey Friday, they sat on packing crates with cinnamon buns to check in. Anders admitted he had almost let a label change slide without mentioning it, then remembered the sheet and sent a short message instead. Omar laughed. "I noticed. It took five minutes to fix." They agreed the rule had held, and added one line: tell the curator together when plans shift. Walking out into the drizzle, Omar said the whole mess in spring had taught them one thing: say it sooner.

qa.q: What does Anders own, according to the sheet?
qa.a: Anders owns layout and the loan paperwork.

qa.q: What does Anders's short message suggest about how he now feels about raising concerns?
qa.a: He feels more at ease speaking up early, trusting that a small concern will be welcomed rather than start a fight.

qa.q: Which part of their agreement seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: The two-day rule, because small concerns get raised while they are still cheap to fix instead of building up for months.

qa.q: What is it like for Omar when a concern arrives early?
qa.a: For Omar it is easy and even funny, a five-minute fix instead of another mess like the one in spring.

grounding: Shows two colleagues with clear ownership, shared credit and an early-warning rule, checking in after a month and drawing the lesson to speak sooner.
